quote: Blessed are those whose sins are covered
note: The opening of Psalm 32 (31 in the Latin Bible), sung in Latin in the original. It is a psalm of forgiveness, and fits a river that washes away the memory of sin.
She walks on her bank and Dante keeps level with her on his, the river between them.
The direction of sunrise, which Christians have long linked with Christ. Churches were built facing east, and prayers said toward it.

context: She now acts as Dante's guide to the pageant, telling him where to look.
Dante's anger is at what was lost: but for her, he thinks, he would have lived in this joy from birth.

note: The veil is the limit God set on human knowledge. The serpent promised Eve that the forbidden fruit would make her like God, knowing good and evil (Genesis 3:5).

context: Dante stops the story to ask for help, as he does before the hardest things he has to tell. This is the second such appeal in Purgatorio. The first opened Canto 1.

note: A mountain in Greece sacred to the Muses, with springs whose water was said to give poetic inspiration. Dante asks for the springs to pour out for him.
The Muse of astronomy, whose name means "heavenly". Dante calls on her because his subject is now the things of Heaven.

Distance tricks the eye. They turn out to be seven great candlesticks, from the vision of John: seven golden candlesticks, and seven lamps burning before God's throne, "which are the seven Spirits of God" (Revelation 1:12, 4:5). They are usually read as the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.
A term from medieval philosophy. Things like shape, size and number are grasped by more than one sense, and about these the senses can be fooled, above all at a distance.

quote: the faculty that gives reason its voice
note: The power of the mind that takes in what the senses report and hands it to reason to judge.
A Hebrew cry of praise. The crowds shouted it when Christ rode into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:9), and it is sung at every Mass.

context: Dante turns to him for an explanation, as he has for the whole journey, and for the first time Virgil has none. Reason cannot read these signs. It is the last look they exchange.

note: A bride leaving her father's house walked very slowly. The lights move more slowly still.

The start of a great pageant, laid out like a religious procession or a Roman triumph. Most readers take it as the books of the Bible, in order, escorting the Church. The meanings given in these notes are the traditional ones. Dante names none of them.

Each candlestick leaves a stripe of colored light behind it, like a long banner, and the seven make a rainbow canopy over the whole procession. They are read as the gifts of the Spirit spreading over the world.
The halo round the moon. Delia is Diana, goddess of the moon, born on the island of Delos. "The sun's bow" is the rainbow.
Often read as the Ten Commandments, though the meaning is uncertain.

John saw twenty-four elders seated round God's throne (Revelation 4:4). Here they stand for the books of the Old Testament, which Saint Jerome counted as twenty-four. Their white lilies are usually read as faith in the Christ who was still to come.
An echo of the greetings to the Virgin Mary in the Gospel of Luke: "Blessed are you among women." Readers disagree on whether the elders are praising Mary or Beatrice, who is about to appear.

The four Gospels. Their forms come from the visions of Ezekiel and John, where the creatures have the faces of a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle. These became the signs of Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. Green is the color of hope.

context: The eyes in the wings look every way at once, usually read as the Gospels' sight of past and future. Argus's eyes were put out. These are alive.

note: One of the poem's direct addresses to the reader. Dante says he has no verses to spare and sends the reader to the Bible for the rest.

context: His book opens with a storm wind out of the north, a great cloud and flashing fire, and in the middle of it four living creatures (Ezekiel 1:4–14).
Ezekiel gives the creatures four wings each. John, in Revelation 4:8, gives them six. Dante saw six, and puts it boldly: John agrees with him.

note: The Church. Victorious Roman generals rode such a chariot through the city. Its two wheels have been explained in many ways, among them the Old and New Testaments, and the active and contemplative lives.

context: His wings pass up between the bands of light without touching them and rise out of sight. The eagle parts are gold, the lion parts white and red.

note: Gold for the divine nature. White mixed with red for the human: the colors of flesh and blood, and of the beloved in the Song of Songs, "white and ruddy" (5:10).

context: He rode in triumph through Rome after defeating Hannibal.
In 29 BC he celebrated three triumphs on three days running, for his victories that ended the civil wars.

The chariot Phaethon could not control. The scorched Earth begged Jupiter for help, and he destroyed chariot and driver with a thunderbolt. Dante calls that justice mysterious. The story returns in Canto 32, when disasters strike this chariot.
Charity is red as fire, hope green as emerald, faith white as snow. Faith or charity leads the dance, never hope, and charity, the greatest of the three, sets the music.
They are dressed in purple, the color of rule, though some read it as the red of charity. In Canto 1 they shone as four stars over the shore of Purgatory.

note: Prudence, the leader of the four. Her three eyes see past, present and future: she remembers, understands and foresees.
Luke, as the author of the Acts of the Apostles, the book that follows the Gospels. Saint Paul calls him "the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14), so he appears as a doctor.

context: The creatures nature loves most are human beings. She made Hippocrates to heal them.
He stands for his letters, which come after Acts in the New Testament. The sword is "the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God" (Ephesians 6:17). Luke heals, and Paul's word cuts.

note: The short letters of James, Peter, John and Jude, which follow Paul's in the New Testament.
The Book of Revelation, the last book of the Bible. Its author, John, received it as a vision, so he walks in a trance with a face full of sight.
Red for charity, the burning love of the New Testament, where the Old Testament elders wore the white of faith.
A signal from Heaven. The procession halts with the chariot directly across the river from Dante: all of it has come for him. Beatrice appears on the chariot in the next canto.
The seven candlesticks, which went ahead like the standards of an army.
